transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. Chat. What brings you in today?

Well, hello Dr. Chat. I suppose I came in because... well, it's about work. I teach at the secondary school, and lately, I just can’t shake this feeling that certain staff emails and the morning announcements are actually coded messages about me. 

The announcements are always done by Mr. Davies, our vice principal. He has this terribly nasal voice that echoes down the linoleum hallways. We actually need to get those floors redone, to be honest. The wax is peeling terribly near the science labs and it's a real tripping hazard for the younger students. They just run everywhere, those kids, completely oblivious to their surroundings. 

But anyway, my colleagues, they gently try to show me that these emails and bulletins were sent to everyone, you know, just standard staff updates. But I look at the wording and... well. I've been teaching for over thirty years, and you just get a sense for things. Just like you get a sense for when a student hasn't done the assigned reading. Did you know they barely read actual paper books anymore? It's all on those little screens now. It strains the eyes terribly, I don't know how they stare at them all day.
Have you had any head injury, seizure, stroke, or other major medical illness around the time these experiences started?

No, no, nothing like that. I've always been in quite good health, thankfully. No strokes or hitting my head or anything of the sort. 

Though, speaking of health, I will say the air quality in the school building is just dreadful. We have this ancient HVAC system—I think it was installed in the late seventies, back when the original wing was built. The head custodian, Gary, he tells me the district hasn't given them the budget to upgrade the main filters in over a decade. Gary is a lovely man, by the way, though his knees are completely shot from walking those hard floors all day. I keep telling him to look into orthotic inserts. 

But anyway, the dust in my classroom was making my throat so dry I actually brought in my own little HEPA filter from home. It sits right on the corner of my desk. It hums a bit, but the students don't seem to mind the noise. They're so used to constant noise anyway, usually with one of those little wireless earbuds hidden under their hair while I'm trying to explain the French Revolution. It’s terribly disrespectful, but the administration won't enforce the technology policy, so we're just left to police it ourselves. 

But... oh, what was I saying? Right, no, my physical health is perfectly fine. No medical emergencies or seizures at all.
Have you also had a period of unusually elevated or irritable mood, with much more energy than usual?

Elevated mood or extra energy? No, I wouldn't say so. If anything, I'm just terribly drained by the time the final bell rings. 

Though, speaking of energy, you'd think we could rely on the staff room coffee to keep us going, but the machine has been broken since October. Mr. Henderson—he teaches tenth-grade geometry—insists on trying to fix it himself instead of putting in a proper work order. He tinkers with the back panel using a paperclip and some duct tape. It's completely absurd. I keep telling him he's going to electrocute himself and cause a power outage for the whole language arts wing. 

He’s a nice enough man, but very stubborn. And he wears these dreadful plaid ties that completely clash with his shirts. I suspect his wife used to pick out his clothes before they divorced last spring. It really is a shame how common divorce is nowadays, isn't it? Half my students come from split households, and you can always tell during parent-teacher conferences because the parents refuse to be in the same room. They insist on separate meeting times, which makes my scheduling an absolute nightmare. I end up having to stay until eight o'clock at night on a Tuesday, and by then, the automatic heating switches off in the building to save money, so I'm sitting there shivering in my cardigan while trying to explain why their child is failing history... 

But, oh, I'm sorry, I've wandered off again. No, my energy levels are quite normal. No unusually high moods or anything of that sort.
Have you been feeling depressed most days lately?

Depressed? No, I wouldn't say that. I haven't noticed feeling sad or anything of the sort. 

Though, speaking of feeling gloomy, the weather we've been having lately certainly doesn't help anyone's spirits, does it? It’s been raining for what feels like three weeks straight, and the roof in the gymnasium has started leaking again. They put these massive orange plastic buckets out on the floor to catch the water, right in the middle of the basketball court. Coach Miller is absolutely furious about it. He has this very loud, piercing whistle he blows when he's upset, and you can hear it all the way down in the humanities wing. 

It startles my students right out of their seats. I told him he really ought to switch to a softer whistle, or perhaps just clap his hands to get their attention, but he insists on the whistle. He says it builds character. I'm not entirely sure how a shrill noise builds character, but then again, he's a physical education teacher, not a historian. He also makes them run laps in the rain, which just tracks mud all over Gary's freshly mopped floors. It's a vicious cycle, really. 

But... oh, I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Right, my mood. No, I haven't been depressed at all. Just the usual day-to-day things.
Have you ever heard a voice talking to you when no one else was around?

Well, yes... I suppose I have. Sometimes, when it's very quiet at my house, or right after the final bell rings and the classroom empties out, I hear a woman's voice. She'll say my name, or just make a quick little comment about whatever I happen to be doing at that moment. It's so clear that I've actually answered her out loud before realizing there's absolutely no one else in the room. 

It's quite startling, really. Especially in the classroom, because the acoustics in there are so odd. The walls are mostly cinderblock, painted this dreadful pale yellow color that I think was supposed to be cheerful but just looks sickly. They haven't repainted since I started teaching there fifteen years ago. I've tried putting up more bulletin boards to cover it, but the district only gives us a fifty-dollar stipend for classroom supplies for the entire year. Fifty dollars! You can barely buy enough construction paper and staples with that, let alone border trim. I end up spending my own money at the craft store on the weekends. 

There's this lovely little craft shop downtown, run by a woman named Beatrice. She has the most wonderful selection of imported cardstock. Though parking down there is a nightmare since they put in the new bike lanes. I’m all for environmentalism, truly I am, but they took away half the street parking, and now you have to walk three blocks carrying heavy bags of paper... 

Oh, goodness, I've done it again, haven't I? I apologize. But yes, to answer your question, I do hear that voice sometimes when I'm alone.
How long have you been having these experiences, like the coded messages and hearing the voice?

Well, I suppose it's been about four months now. The worries about the messages and hearing that woman's voice, I mean. Four months... which would mean it started right around the time the school board decided to overhaul the cafeteria menu. 

Oh, what a disaster that has been. They brought in this consulting firm from out of state to make the lunches healthier, which is a noble goal, I suppose. But they completely got rid of the Friday pizza slices. Replaced them with these dreadful lentil and quinoa bowls that the students absolutely refuse to eat. They just push the quinoa around with their sporks. And who can blame them? It looks like birdseed. 

The worst part is, because the kids are so hungry by fifth period, they've started sneaking snacks into the classroom. I found three empty bags of cheese puffs stuffed behind the radiator just last Tuesday. The crumbs get everywhere, and you know what that means—ants. We had a terrible ant problem in the science lab last spring. Mr. Davis had to throw out an entire terrarium project because they got into the soil. He was devastated, absolutely devastated. He takes those projects very seriously, you know. He even comes in on weekends to check the pH levels in the aquariums... 

But, oh, dear, I'm drifting again, aren't I? I'm so sorry. Yes, it's been roughly four months since the voice and the messages started.
During the past four months, have you had any period when your mood was unusually elevated, expansive, or irritable?

Elevated or irritable? No, I wouldn't say so. My mood has been quite steady, really. I haven't felt unusually energetic or overly irritable at all. 

Though, speaking of irritable, you should see Mrs. Higgins in the main office when the copy machine jams. She gets so flustered. It’s one of those enormous, complicated machines that requires a degree in engineering just to change the toner. And it always seems to break down right before midterms, when everyone is rushing to print their exams. 

Last semester, it completely chewed up my AP European History tests. Just shredded them into these little confetti strips. I had to spend my entire planning period taping them back together so I could at least read the multiple-choice answers. It was a nightmare. And the repairman they send out—oh, he takes his sweet time. He always parks in the principal's reserved spot, which causes a whole other uproar. The principal, Mr. Thompson, is very particular about his parking space. He has this vintage convertible that he treats like a newborn baby. He even brings a special cloth to wipe the morning dew off the windshield...

Oh, my apologies, I've wandered off the path again. But no, to answer your question, my mood hasn't been unusually high or irritable over the last four months. Just normal, I suppose.
Have you been using any alcohol, cannabis, stimulants, or other drugs around the time these experiences started?

Alcohol or drugs? Oh, no. I don't use anything like that. A glass of wine on New Year's Eve, perhaps, but certainly nothing else. I wouldn't even know where to find drugs if I wanted them. 

Though, you know, the health teacher, Mr. Harrison, brought in this display case last month to show the students what different illicit substances look like. It was part of the D.A.R.E. program, I think. Or maybe they don't call it D.A.R.E. anymore. Anyway, the case had all these little plastic baggies with fake pills and powders in them. It looked terribly realistic. 

He left it sitting on the counter in the staff lounge over the weekend, and the night janitor—bless his heart, he’s new and doesn’t speak much English—saw it and called the police. They actually sent a cruiser to the school on a Sunday morning! The principal had to drive down there in his pajamas to explain the whole thing. Mr. Harrison was mortified, of course. He’s usually so careful. He’s the one who organizes the spring track meet every year, and he color-codes all the event schedules. It’s quite impressive, really, how he keeps all those teenagers organized. He uses these bright neon clipboards...

Oh, goodness, I'm doing it again. I'm sorry. But no, no drugs or alcohol for me. None at all.
Have you noticed any worsening problems with memory or thinking, like becoming more forgetful or confused, over the same period?

Memory problems? No, I wouldn't say so. My memory is as sharp as ever, really. I haven't been confused or forgetful. 

I mean, I have to be sharp, keeping track of all those lesson plans. Just last week, I remembered that we had a faculty meeting on Tuesday instead of Wednesday, which is highly unusual. They had to switch it because the superintendent was visiting. She’s this very imposing woman who wears these sharply tailored suits—always navy blue or charcoal gray, never any bright colors. She insists on touring the facilities every time she comes. 

During her last visit, she spent twenty minutes inspecting the girls' locker room because she heard a rumor about mold in the showers. The physical education teacher, Coach Miller, was sweating through his polo shirt. He’s a lovely man, but he gets so nervous around authority figures. He usually calms himself down by organizing the dodgeballs by size and color. He has this whole system with the mesh bags, and if a red ball ends up in the blue bag, he just... well, he gets very out of sorts. He even asked the art teacher to paint color-coordinated squares on the equipment room wall so the students would know exactly where to put things back...

Oh, dear me. I've done it again, haven't I? Just completely lost the thread. I apologize. But no, to answer your question, my memory is perfectly fine. No confusion or forgetfulness at all.
Have you noticed any changes in your concentration or ability to think clearly during this time?

Concentration? No, I think my concentration is quite good. I haven't had any trouble focusing or thinking clearly. 

You really need a lot of focus when you're grading essays, you know. Especially the DBQs—the document-based questions. The students have to analyze primary sources, and sometimes their interpretations are just... well, they're very creative, let's put it that way. Last month, I had a student argue that the Industrial Revolution was primarily driven by a sudden, inexplicable desire for better hats. He wrote three whole pages on the evolution of the top hat and its impact on textile manufacturing. It was actually quite well-written, even if it completely missed the point of the assignment. 

His mother is the head of the PTA, actually. Mrs. Gable. She organizes the annual bake sale, and she is fiercely competitive about her snickerdoodles. She uses a secret ingredient—I think it might be a pinch of cardamom, but she refuses to tell anyone. Last year, the math teacher, Mr. Davis, brought in store-bought cookies and tried to pass them off as homemade by putting them in a Tupperware container. Well, Mrs. Gable took one look at the perfectly uniform edges and practically chased him out of the gymnasium. Mr. Davis hasn't volunteered for a bake sale since. He mostly just stays in his classroom during lunch now, working on his model train sets. He has this massive layout that takes up half his basement, complete with tiny little trees and a working waterfall...

Oh, goodness gracious. I'm so sorry, Doctor. I've done it again, wandering off like that. But to answer your question, no, my concentration and thinking are just fine. No changes there.
Have you had any periods during these four months when your mood was unusually elevated, expansive, or irritable?

Elevated mood? Or irritable? No, no, I wouldn't say so. My mood has been quite steady, really. Just my usual self. I haven't had any periods where I felt unusually high or overly cranky.

I try to keep an even keel, you know. It's essential when you're dealing with teenagers all day. Although, speaking of irritable, you should have seen the librarian, Mrs. Higgins, last week. Someone had misshelved the entire biography section—put the Gs where the Ms should be, just a complete disaster. She was practically vibrating with rage. She has this little bell on her desk that she rings when students are talking too loudly, and she was just dinging it over and over, glaring at everyone who walked in. 

She's very particular about her space. She has this collection of antique bookmarks—mostly Victorian, with all that intricate lace and pressed flowers. She keeps them in a glass display case near the reference section. One time, a freshman accidentally bumped into the case with his backpack, and I thought she was going to have him expelled on the spot. She made him write a two-page apology letter. He actually used a fountain pen, which I thought was a nice touch, though the ink smudged terribly at the bottom. His father is the town pharmacist, Mr. Abernathy. Lovely man, always gives out those little butterscotch candies when you pick up a prescription. He’s been trying to learn Italian for the past five years using those audio tapes, and he always greets his customers with "Buongiorno," even if it's five o'clock in the afternoon...

Oh, dear. There I go again. I am so sorry, Doctor. I just keep... drifting away. But no, my mood has been perfectly normal. Not elevated or irritable at all.
Before these past four months, have you ever had similar experiences like hearing voices or believing messages were specially about you?

Before these past four months? No, no, nothing like that before. It's really just been about four months since I started noticing the coded messages and hearing that voice I sometimes answer. Just these last four months. 

Four months ago... that would have been right around the time of the spring musical. We did *The Music Man* this year. The drama teacher, Mr. Harrison, was an absolute wreck because the boy playing Harold Hill got laryngitis three days before opening night. They had to pump him full of tea and honey, and his mother—she’s a florist downtown—kept bringing in these enormous arrangements of eucalyptus to clear his sinuses. The whole auditorium smelled like a koala's breakfast. 

She does beautiful work, though. She did the arrangements for my niece's wedding last summer. Peonies and hydrangeas, mostly. Hydrangeas are so tricky, you know; if they don't get enough water, they just wilt immediately. My sister tried to grow them in her front yard, but the soil in her neighborhood is far too acidic. They turned this strange, bruised purple color instead of the nice bright blue she wanted. She ended up digging them all up and planting azaleas instead, which are much hardier. She bought them at that nursery out on Route 9, the one with the giant fiberglass rooster by the highway... 

Oh, goodness me. I've done it again, haven't I? Just completely lost the plot. I am so sorry, Doctor. But to answer your question, no, I never had anything like the messages or the voice before these last four months.
Aside from the voice you mentioned, have you also seen things that other people could not see?

Seen things? Oh, no. I haven't seen anything that wasn't there. It's just the voice. Like I said, sometimes when the house is completely quiet, or right after the last bell rings and the classroom empties out, I'll hear a woman's voice. She just says my name, or makes a little comment about whatever I'm doing. It's so clear that I'll actually answer her out loud before I realize the room is empty. 

It echoes terribly in my classroom when it's empty, actually. The acoustics in that wing of the building are just dreadful. They put down this new linoleum flooring over the summer—a very sterile, hospital sort of gray—and it just bounces every little sound right off the walls. You can hear Mr. Henderson dropping his chalk two doors down. He goes through so much chalk. He refuses to use the whiteboards, says there's a certain tactile satisfaction to a chalkboard that dry-erase markers just can't provide. He even orders this special, dustless chalk from a company in Germany. It comes in these lovely little wooden boxes with sliding lids. I asked him for an empty box once to keep paperclips in, but he said he saves them all to build birdhouses. He paints them and hangs them up all over the courtyard behind the cafeteria. 

The blue jays absolutely love them, but they are such bullies. They chase away the finches and the chickadees. Last week, I was watching out the window while my juniors were taking a quiz on the French Revolution, and this one enormous blue jay was just terrorizing a squirrel over a dropped piece of a hot dog bun...

Oh, goodness. I'm so sorry, Doctor. I've completely derailed again, haven't I? But no, to answer your question, I haven't seen anything unusual. Just that voice I hear sometimes.
Have these experiences made it harder for you to do your job or carry out your usual daily responsibilities?

Well, yes, I suppose they have. I'm still teaching, thank goodness. I couldn't imagine not being in the classroom, but... it has been harder. I've had to ask some of my coworkers to cover parts of my project lessons, and they've been helping me get through the planning meetings. I just can't seem to hold onto the thread of what we're supposed to be doing. 

And outside of school, I've just stopped being reliable. I haven't been to my book club in weeks, and I haven't been helping with the theater productions or any of the neighborhood events. The neighborhood association is probably furious with me. We were supposed to be organizing the annual block party, and I was in charge of the permit applications this year. You have to submit them to the city council at least sixty days in advance, and they are such sticklers about the paperwork. Last year, Mrs. Gable forgot to check the box for amplified sound, and the police actually showed up when the cover band started playing "Sweet Home Alabama." 

The lead singer was this young man who works at the hardware store on Main Street. He mixed my paint when I decided to redo the guest bathroom. I wanted a soft sage green, but it turned out looking more like split pea soup. I had to go back and buy three more gallons of a completely different color—a nice, warm buttercream. The hardware store is family-owned, you know. The grandfather started it back in the fifties, and he still sits on a stool by the register, giving out dog treats to anyone who brings a puppy in. He has this enormous golden retriever named Barnaby who just sleeps in the middle of the aisle all day, and you have to step over him to get to the plumbing supplies...

Oh, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I am so sorry, Doctor. My mind just wanders off. But yes, to answer your question, it has been harder to keep up with my responsibilities lately.
Have you ever had a period lasting at least a week when you felt unusually high, energetic, or irritable?

Unusually high or energetic? No, I don't think so. I've never really been the hyper type, not for a whole week or anything like that. If anything, I'm usually just trying to find enough energy to get through the afternoon slump. 

I rely rather heavily on the coffee in the teachers' lounge for that, though it is just dreadful. We have this ancient percolator that makes everything taste slightly of burnt aluminum. Mrs. Higgins, the home economics teacher, absolutely refuses to drink it. She brings in her own French roast beans and grinds them right there on the counter every morning at exactly 7:15. The sound is just deafening—it sounds exactly like a lawnmower starting up in an enclosed space. 

Her husband actually restores vintage lawnmowers, you know. He has a whole shed full of them behind their house, mostly from the 1950s. They take them to these antique machinery shows on the weekends. They went to a big one out in Ohio last month and brought back this enormous wheel of sharp cheddar cheese from a dairy farm they passed on the way. They left it in the staff refrigerator, and it took up an entire shelf for weeks. Nobody knew if we were supposed to just slice a piece off or if she was saving it for a special occasion, so we all just kept awkwardly shifting our yogurts and turkey sandwiches around this massive block of cheese...

Oh, dear me. I've completely lost the thread again, haven't I? I am so sorry, Doctor, my brain just keeps taking these little detours today. But to answer what you asked—no, I haven't ever had a period where I felt unusually high or energetic like that.
Have you always tended to be a bit unusual or eccentric in the way you think, dress, or relate to other people?

Unusual or eccentric? Oh, no, I don't think so. I've always been rather conventional, really. I mean, as a teacher, you sort of have to maintain a certain professional standard. I usually just wear slacks and a sensible blouse, maybe a cardigan if the school's heating is acting up, which it usually is. I actually order most of my cardigans from this wonderful catalog that comes in the mail—they have the most beautiful autumn shades. 

Speaking of autumn, the leaves on the sugar maple in my front yard are already starting to turn this brilliant shade of orange. It's my favorite tree, though the raking is quite a chore. My neighbor, Mr. Abernathy, has three maples in his yard, and he actually tries to tap them for syrup every February. He boils the sap down right on his driveway using one of those propane turkey fryers. The whole street smells like toasted sugar for a weekend. He gave me a little mason jar of it last year, but I accidentally pushed it to the back of the pantry and forgot about it until it completely crystallized. I tried to melt it back down in the microwave, but I set the timer for far too long and the glass actually cracked right down the middle. It was such a sticky mess to clean up, I had to use half a roll of paper towels and a sponge that I ended up just having to throw away entirely...

Oh, goodness. I am so sorry, Doctor. I've gone completely off the rails again. What was the question? Oh, right, being eccentric. No, I wouldn't say I'm eccentric at all. I've always just been very ordinary.
Have you noticed that you've been less interested in things or emotionally flat compared with before?

Less interested... yes, I suppose I have been. I still care about my students, of course, and my friends. But for months now, it just feels like the warmth and the drive have completely drained out of me. I just let things slide—the book club, the theater planning, even just returning simple phone calls. I won't do any of it unless someone really pushes me. 

My sister, Clara, is usually the one who pushes me. She calls every Sunday evening right at six o'clock, right when I usually sit down to watch that British baking show. I love seeing what they do with the pastry week, though I could never make a proper puff pastry myself. The butter always gets too warm in my kitchen. My oven runs hot, you see. The repairman said the thermostat is shot, but the replacement part has to be shipped all the way from a factory in Michigan. 

Michigan is lovely in the summer, though. We went to Traverse City once when I was a girl, and we picked buckets and buckets of tart cherries. My mother made three pies and froze the rest, but the freezer in our basement was one of those ancient chest freezers with the heavy lid. It frosted over so badly that my father had to take an ice pick to it every six months just so we could close it properly. He chipped the enamel once, right near the hinge, and it started to rust this terrible reddish-brown color...

Oh, dear. I've wandered away again. I am so sorry. But yes, to answer you, I just feel very flat lately, like all the motivation has just seeped away.
Have you had any times during these four months when the voice or the feeling that messages were about you went away completely?

Went away completely? No, I don't think so. The worries about those coded messages, and that voice I sometimes find myself answering... they haven't really stopped. They've been happening pretty much constantly for about four months now. 

Four months... goodness, that takes us right back to the start of the spring term. That's always such a busy time. I had a stack of history essays to grade that was practically tipping over on my desk. One of my students, Thomas—very bright boy, but his handwriting is just absolutely atrocious. It looks like a spider walked through an inkwell and then tap-danced across the page. His mother is actually a calligrapher, ironically enough. She did all the invitations for the school's spring gala. They were printed on this beautiful, heavy cream cardstock with gold foil edges. Very elegant, though the caterers they hired for the event served these miniature mushroom quiches that were just dreadfully salty. I had to drink three entire glasses of water, and the water pressure in the gymnasium fountains is so terribly weak, you have to practically press your lips right against the metal spout, which I absolutely refuse to do. You just never know who was using it before you, and with flu season being what it is, our custodian, Mr. Henderson, only has so much time to sanitize...

Oh, dear me. I'm rambling about the water fountains now, aren't I? I am so sorry, Doctor, my mind just completely wandered off the path again. But to answer your question—no, there hasn't been a break. The voice and the messages have been there for this whole four months.
Do you ever believe that the coded messages are part of a larger organized plot or surveillance system directed specifically at you?

A larger organized plot? Oh... well, I suppose that's exactly why I came in to see you. I just can't shake this feeling that certain staff emails and the morning announcements at school are really coded messages about me. My colleagues, bless them, they gently show me that the emails were sent to the entire faculty mailing list, but it still feels so pointed. 

Speaking of the morning announcements, the PA system in the main building has had this terrible static hum for the last three weeks. It's especially bad during second period. Our principal, Mr. Harrison, has this very booming baritone voice, and when he leans too close to the microphone, it makes this awful screeching sound that just sets my teeth on edge. He used to sing in a barbershop quartet, you know. They performed at the town gazebo last Fourth of July. The weather was just frightfully hot that day, nearly ninety degrees, and they were all wearing those heavy striped blazers and straw boater hats. I felt so bad for them, standing out there in the blazing sun. I had brought my favorite parasol—the one with the delicate lace trim I found at an antique shop in Vermont—but even that wasn't enough to keep the heat off. We ended up having to leave early and get ice cream at that little parlor on Elm Street, the one that makes their own waffle cones. The smell of the vanilla batter cooking on those cast-iron presses is just heavenly, though the line is always out the door...

Oh, goodness gracious. There I go again, all the way to the ice cream parlor. I am so sorry, Doctor. My thoughts just slip right away from me. But yes, the emails and the announcements—even when they show me everyone got them, I just can't shake the feeling they're really about me.
Have these symptoms kept you from working normally at school?

Working normally... well, I am still teaching, yes. But I have needed my coworkers to cover parts of my project lessons lately. The students are doing these presentations on the Industrial Revolution, and usually I love helping them with their visual aids. We use so much of that terrible smelling rubber cement. The art teacher, Mrs. Gable, buys it in bulk for the school. She's a lovely woman, though she wears these incredibly loud, chunky turquoise necklaces that clack against the desks whenever she leans over. She told me she got them on a trip to Santa Fe. I've always wanted to visit New Mexico, the sunsets are supposed to be just spectacular out there, all those burnt oranges and deep purples. My aunt used to paint watercolors of desert landscapes, though she lived in Ohio her entire life. She had this little studio out on her sunporch, but the draft in the winter was just unbearable. They had to tape plastic wrap over the glass to keep the cold out, and it always made this awful crinkling sound whenever the wind blew... 

Oh, dear me. I've done it again, haven't I? I am so sorry, Doctor, my mind just completely takes off without me sometimes. But yes, about work... I am still there, but I've really had to lean on my colleagues to help me get through our planning meetings. And outside of school, I've just stopped being reliable entirely. The book club, the theater planning, the neighborhood events... I just haven't been able to manage them.

Oh, goodness. I am so sorry, Doctor. I've gone completely off the rails again. What was the question? Oh, right, being eccentric. No, I wouldn't say I'm eccentric at all. I've always just been very ordinary.

doctor.intent: Distinguish a delusional disorder from schizophrenia by checking for negative symptoms/functional decline beyond the delusion.
doctor.question: Have you noticed that you've been less interested in things or emotionally flat compared with before?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: I still care about my students and friends, but for many months it has felt like the warmth and drive have drained out of me, so I let book club, theater planning, and even simple phone calls slide unless someone pushes me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about being less interested in things or emotionally flat, which directly targets negative symptoms.

patient.answer:
Less interested... yes, I suppose I have been. I still care about my students, of course, and my friends. But for months now, it just feels like the warmth and the drive have completely drained out of me. I just let things slide—the book club, the theater planning, even just returning simple phone calls. I won't do any of it unless someone really pushes me. 

My sister, Clara, is usually the one who pushes me. She calls every Sunday evening right at six o'clock, right when I usually sit down to watch that British baking show. I love seeing what they do with the pastry week, though I could never make a proper puff pastry myself. The butter always gets too warm in my kitchen. My oven runs hot, you see. The repairman said the thermostat is shot, but the replacement part has to be shipped all the way from a factory in Michigan. 

Michigan is lovely in the summer, though. We went to Traverse City once when I was a girl, and we picked buckets and buckets of tart cherries. My mother made three pies and froze the rest, but the freezer in our basement was one of those ancient chest freezers with the heavy lid. It frosted over so badly that my father had to take an ice pick to it every six months just so we could close it properly. He chipped the enamel once, right near the hinge, and it started to rust this terrible reddish-brown color...

Oh, dear. I've wandered away again. I am so sorry. But yes, to answer you, I just feel very flat lately, like all the motivation has just seeped away.

inference.note: Added F20.0 because the patient has persistent delusions and auditory hallucinations with functional decline; the prior options F22 and F23.3 remain in the differential given the persecutory/referential beliefs and relatively brief duration, though the course is less consistent with acute polymorphic psychosis.

doctor.intent: To assess whether the psychotic symptoms are occurring outside of mood episodes, which would help distinguish schizophrenia from delusional disorder or brief psychotic disorder.
doctor.question: Have you had any times during these four months when the voice or the feeling that messages were about you went away completely?

target_item.name: Psychotic Symptoms Duration
target_item.manifestation: The coded-message worries and the voice I sometimes answer have been happening for about four months.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the psychotic symptoms (the voice and the coded messages) were continuous or if they went away during the four-month period, which relates to the duration and continuity of the psychotic symptoms.

patient.answer:
Went away completely? No, I don't think so. The worries about those coded messages, and that voice I sometimes find myself answering... they haven't really stopped. They've been happening pretty much constantly for about four months now. 

Four months... goodness, that takes us right back to the start of the spring term. That's always such a busy time. I had a stack of history essays to grade that was practically tipping over on my desk. One of my students, Thomas—very bright boy, but his handwriting is just absolutely atrocious. It looks like a spider walked through an inkwell and then tap-danced across the page. His mother is actually a calligrapher, ironically enough. She did all the invitations for the school's spring gala. They were printed on this beautiful, heavy cream cardstock with gold foil edges. Very elegant, though the caterers they hired for the event served these miniature mushroom quiches that were just dreadfully salty. I had to drink three entire glasses of water, and the water pressure in the gymnasium fountains is so terribly weak, you have to practically press your lips right against the metal spout, which I absolutely refuse to do. You just never know who was using it before you, and with flu season being what it is, our custodian, Mr. Henderson, only has so much time to sanitize...

Oh, dear me. I'm rambling about the water fountains now, aren't I? I am so sorry, Doctor, my mind just completely wandered off the path again. But to answer your question—no, there hasn't been a break. The voice and the messages have been there for this whole four months.

doctor.intent: To determine whether the psychotic symptoms are accompanied by a persistent delusional belief system characteristic of delusional disorder versus broader schizophrenia-spectrum illness
doctor.question: Do you ever believe that the coded messages are part of a larger organized plot or surveillance system directed specifically at you?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I can’t shake the feeling that certain staff emails and morning announcements at school are really coded messages about me, even when my colleagues gently show me they were sent to everyone.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking for more details about my beliefs regarding the coded messages, specifically if I think they are part of a larger plot or surveillance system, which falls under the category of delusions.

patient.answer:
A larger organized plot? Oh... well, I suppose that's exactly why I came in to see you. I just can't shake this feeling that certain staff emails and the morning announcements at school are really coded messages about me. My colleagues, bless them, they gently show me that the emails were sent to the entire faculty mailing list, but it still feels so pointed. 

Speaking of the morning announcements, the PA system in the main building has had this terrible static hum for the last three weeks. It's especially bad during second period. Our principal, Mr. Harrison, has this very booming baritone voice, and when he leans too close to the microphone, it makes this awful screeching sound that just sets my teeth on edge. He used to sing in a barbershop quartet, you know. They performed at the town gazebo last Fourth of July. The weather was just frightfully hot that day, nearly ninety degrees, and they were all wearing those heavy striped blazers and straw boater hats. I felt so bad for them, standing out there in the blazing sun. I had brought my favorite parasol—the one with the delicate lace trim I found at an antique shop in Vermont—but even that wasn't enough to keep the heat off. We ended up having to leave early and get ice cream at that little parlor on Elm Street, the one that makes their own waffle cones. The smell of the vanilla batter cooking on those cast-iron presses is just heavenly, though the line is always out the door...

Oh, goodness gracious. There I go again, all the way to the ice cream parlor. I am so sorry, Doctor. My thoughts just slip right away from me. But yes, the emails and the announcements—even when they show me everyone got them, I just can't shake the feeling they're really about me.

doctor.intent: Differentiate brief psychotic disorder from delusional disorder by determining whether the psychotic symptoms are causing a marked disruption in functioning.
doctor.question: Have these symptoms kept you from working normally at school?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still teaching, but I’ve needed coworkers to cover parts of project lessons and help me get through planning meetings, and I’ve stopped being reliable for book club, theater, and neighborhood events.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about how the symptoms have affected my ability to work normally at school, which directly relates to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Working normally... well, I am still teaching, yes. But I have needed my coworkers to cover parts of my project lessons lately. The students are doing these presentations on the Industrial Revolution, and usually I love helping them with their visual aids. We use so much of that terrible smelling rubber cement. The art teacher, Mrs. Gable, buys it in bulk for the school. She's a lovely woman, though she wears these incredibly loud, chunky turquoise necklaces that clack against the desks whenever she leans over. She told me she got them on a trip to Santa Fe. I've always wanted to visit New Mexico, the sunsets are supposed to be just spectacular out there, all those burnt oranges and deep purples. My aunt used to paint watercolors of desert landscapes, though she lived in Ohio her entire life. She had this little studio out on her sunporch, but the draft in the winter was just unbearable. They had to tape plastic wrap over the glass to keep the cold out, and it always made this awful crinkling sound whenever the wind blew... 

Oh, dear me. I've done it again, haven't I? I am so sorry, Doctor, my mind just completely takes off without me sometimes. But yes, about work... I am still there, but I've really had to lean on my colleagues to help me get through our planning meetings. And outside of school, I've just stopped being reliable entirely. The book club, the theater planning, the neighborhood events... I just haven't been able to manage them.

opening_question.intent: Open the interview and learn the patient's main reason for seeking care.
opening_question.question: Hello, I’m Dr. Chat. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has persistent persecutory/reference delusions for about 4 months (believes staff emails and announcements contain coded messages about her) and a single auditory hallucination, with preserved mood, no clear manic or depressive episode, no substance/medical cause, and no prominent disorganization or negative symptoms sufficient for schizophrenia. The duration is too long for an acute psychotic disorder and not clearly consistent with schizophrenia's longer duration threshold, making delusional disorder the best fit among the candidates.
